extracted.intended_audience: researchers in communication/journalism, media scholars, and practitioners interested in online news selection (e.g., news editors, UX designers)
extracted.subtask_description: An experimental study of how journalistic news factors (e.g., reach, controversy) and popularity indicators (specifically comment counts) influence users' selection of news teasers on a fictitious news website. The paper describes operationalizations, manipulations, measurement items, sampling, and statistical analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: News factors (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: News factors refer to characteristics or qualities of news stories (for example, the degree of damage reported or the status of the people involved). They serve as selection criteria that increase a story's newsworthiness—the likelihood that the story will be selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined as characteristics/qualities of news; news values are journalists' judgments about these factors. The two-component theory (Kepplinger & Ehmig, 2006) distinguishes news factors (story characteristics) from news values (journalistic judgments). Eilders (1997) reformulation: 'The higher the intensity of a news factor within a news item is, the more likely that this news item is used by the audience.' Use of news factors as general relevance indicators; higher intensity expected to increase selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversy / Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayal of disagreement, opposing views, or conflict in a news item (labeled 'controversy' in the study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized as high vs low intensity in teasers (e.g., 'Protests against methane extraction escalating' vs 'Environmental experts warning against methane extraction'). Chosen because prior research shows controversy affects users' selection; in this study higher controversy intensity prompted more clicks (65% vs 35% when controversy intensity higher). Measured via item: 'The teaser is all about conflict.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of persons affected by an event; social relevance in terms of how many people are concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized as high vs low intensity in teasers (e.g., 'Amount of pertussis infections at a record level' vs 'Amount of pertussis infections slightly gone up'). Prior research shows reach affects selection; in this study higher reach intensity prompted more clicks (62% vs 38% when reach intensity higher). Measured via item: 'The topic concerns many people.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Damage
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative consequences reported in a story; extent of harm or damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as a news factor with strong impact in prior empirical studies; mentioned as an example of a news factor that often shows marked influence on selection. Not manipulated in this experiment but flagged as a significant factor in the news-factors literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: References to established issues or ongoing relevance of a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named among news factors that have repeatedly shown impact in different settings. Mentioned as a potential relevance indicator for audiences; not directly manipulated here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation of information in human terms (e.g., focusing on people rather than abstractions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a news factor with repeated empirical impact in prior studies. Not directly manipulated in this study but recognized as a selection criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values (journalistic judgments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of journalists—their judgment about the relevance of news factors (how news factors increase newsworthiness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News values are distinct from news factors: factors are story characteristics; values are journalists' judgments about those factors. This distinction underlies the theoretical framing that journalists' relevance criteria (news values) and audience selection can operate similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popularity indicators / news cues (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregated information about other users' behavior embedded in teasers (e.g., number of clicks, shares, user comments, recommendations, likes, diggs, 'most viewed' rankings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered alternative selection criteria for users and explained via dual-process models (ELM) as triggers of heuristics. Can function differently depending on type (clicks vs shares vs comments). Empirical findings are mixed across studies; popularity indicators may influence attention, perceived credibility, perceived newsworthiness, click likelihood, and sharing intention in some contexts (e.g., Xu 2013) but not in others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment count (specific popularity indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of user comments displayed with a news teaser (manipulated here as 'high' vs 'low').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesized to trigger the bandwagon heuristic (RQ1). Operationalized with low = 1–9 comments and high = 49–62 comments in the main experiment (pretests used somewhat lower high counts). In this study, comment counts did not affect selection (chi-square p = .082); authors discuss possible reasons—comment counts may reflect selective participation rather than reception/multiplication, may require higher thresholds or show nonlinear/curvilinear effects, and may be processed differently than clicks or recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bandwagon heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic whereby individuals infer value from others' behavior: 'If others think that this is a good story, then I should think so too.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain how popularity indicators (news cues) might influence selection under peripheral processing (ELM). Empirical support is mixed; bandwagon perception and perceived newsworthiness can mediate effects of popularity indicators on clicks and sharing in some studies (e.g., Xu, 2013).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of audience-selection behaviors (reception / multiplication / participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorization of audience behaviors reflected by popularity indicators: selective reception (clicks), selective multiplication (recommendations/shares), selective participation (comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important conceptual distinction (Wendelin et al., 2017) because different popularity indicators reflect different user behaviors and may therefore have different meanings and differential influence on selection. Comment counts reflect selective participation and may be less influential on reading choices than indicators of reception or multiplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recency and related-article cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Cues provided by search engines and aggregators such as upload-recency and number-of-related-articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identified as news cues likely to influence selection; part of the broader set of popularity/metadata cues available on online platforms (Sundar et al., 2007).

rubrics_metrics.name: News selection operationalization (click intention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational definition of the dependent variable: intended choice of which teaser to read first (clicking intention among six teasers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants were instructed to imagine normal surfing and click the teaser they'd read first. Reading time was not used because it goes beyond initial selection and can be influenced by unmanipulated article characteristics. Dependent variable coded as selection between three controversy teasers (0) and three reach teasers (1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation checks / measurement items
rubrics_metrics.description: Items used to assess perceived manipulations and controls: e.g., 'The topic concerns many people' (reach), 'The teaser is all about conflict' (controversy), 'Many people commented on this article' (comment count), 'The teaser is formulated clearly and comprehensibly', and 'The content of the teaser is credible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All items scored on 5-point Likert scale from 1 (does not apply at all) to 5 (applies completely). Pretests confirmed differentiation between high/low versions. Manipulation checks used to validate stimulus manipulations and to assess comprehensibility and credibility effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design standards (manipulations and controls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design choices for valid inference: 4×4 mixed design combining two 2×2 designs (controversy intensity × comment count and reach intensity × comment count), fully cross-factorial manipulations, randomization of teaser order, use of three topic domains (politics, advice, sports), fabricated content to control for prior knowledge, and pretests to calibrate intensity differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample quotas aimed for balance across education, gender, and age; between- and within-subject factors used; 16 experimental groups required; manipulation levels chosen (high vs low) because finer gradations did not necessarily strengthen intensity–selection relationships (per literature). Such procedural standards increase external validity while controlling for topic interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covariates to control in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual-level variables included as covariates: sociodemographics, prior news consumption (duration on previous day), and individual comment behavior (frequency of commenting in last six months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: prior experience with news websites and commenting behavior may influence attention to popularity indicators. These variables were included in logistic regression models to account for variance and secure chi-square results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis and reporting standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended analytic approaches used: contingency tables with chi-square tests and phi coefficients; logistic regression controlling for covariates; report odds ratios (ORs), significance (p-values), effect sizes (phi, Nagelkerke's R2), and power (1 − β).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting ORs: >1 indicates increase in probability, <1 decrease. Report overall model significance and explained variance. Note discussion of power limitations (e.g., possible small effects of comment counts needing larger sample to detect). Consider testing for nonlinear (curvilinear) effects where prior studies suggest them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonlinear / threshold considerations for popularity indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Popularity indicators (e.g., click rates or comment counts) may have nonlinear (e.g., curvilinear) effects or require threshold levels before influencing selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note previous findings of curvilinear effects (Knobloch-Westerwick et al., 2005) and suggest that comment counts in this study may have been too low or that an effect is nonlinear; recommend analyzing multiple levels and larger samples to detect such patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative/gatekeeping implication criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether publishing comment counts affects editorial gatekeeping power over what users read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this study's findings, comment counts did not impact selection, suggesting that publishing comment counts alone is insufficient to change the gatekeeping role of editorial selection; if the goal is to encourage comment reading/participation, comment counts alone may not attract attention.
